content.text: A ball thrown in the air traces a path as shown below.

content.alt_text: Dotted positions of a ball at equal time intervals along an arc that rises to a maximum height and then falls back to the launch level.

content.text: Which of the following statements is true?
The velocity of the ball keeps changing.
The acceleration of the ball keeps changing.
The velocity of the ball at the top of its motion is zero.
The acceleration of the ball at the top of its motion is zero.
After release the only force on the ball is its weight, so write down its acceleration and check whether that acceleration changes anywhere along the path.
Then check the velocity at the top of the motion: which *component* of the velocity is zero there, and is the acceleration zero as well?
A

The only force acting once the ball leaves the thrower's hand is its weight, so its acceleration is constant at $g$ downwards and does not change. Because the acceleration has a component along the direction of motion, the vertical component of the velocity changes continuously, so the total velocity keeps changing. At the top of the motion the vertical component of velocity is zero, but the horizontal component is not, so the velocity is not zero; the acceleration is $g$ downwards, not zero.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the velocity of the ball keeps changing because the vertical component of velocity is continuously altered by the constant downward gravitational acceleration (correct response A).

content.text: Why would a satellite in low orbit around Earth eventually fall to Earth?
It is not in a geostationary orbit.
Gravity is too strong at low orbits.
The sun's solar wind pushes it out of orbit.
The upper atmosphere gradually slows it down.
A satellite in orbit is not weightless because gravity is absent; gravity supplies the centripetal force. So something else must be removing energy from the orbit.
Ask whether a satellite in a *low* orbit is still inside the atmosphere, and what a drag force does to its speed. A reduced speed means the satellite can no longer maintain that orbit at that radius.
D

In a low orbit the satellite is still within the upper atmosphere. Air resistance opposes its motion and slowly reduces its orbital speed. With less speed the satellite can no longer maintain that orbit, so gravity pulls it into a lower orbit and it eventually decays to the surface.

items: 1 mark: identifies atmospheric drag in the upper atmosphere as the mechanism that lowers the satellite's orbital speed (correct response D).

content.text: The initial velocity required by a space probe to just escape the gravitational pull of a planet is called escape velocity.
Which of the following quantities does NOT affect the magnitude of the escape velocity?
Mass of the planet
Mass of the space probe
Radius of the planet
Universal gravitational constant
Write the energy condition for marginal escape, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{r}$, then look carefully at what happens to the mass $m$ of the escaping object.
The quantity you are looking for is the one that cancels out of the expression you get for the required speed.
B

$v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$, which depends on the mass $M$ and radius $r$ of the planet and on the universal gravitational constant $G$, but not on the mass of the escaping body. The probe's mass appears in both the kinetic energy and the gravitational potential energy and so cancels out.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the mass of the space probe does not affect the escape velocity (correct response B).

content.text: A space probe, $P$, is in a stable orbit around a small, distant planet. The probe fires a forward-facing rocket that reduces its orbital speed by half.
Which of the following best illustrates the subsequent motion of the probe?

content.alt_text: Diagram A: probe P in a circular orbit with a dashed path that swings out to a much larger orbit, escaping the original orbit.
Diagram B: probe P in a circular orbit with a dashed path that curves inward slightly, remaining in a smaller near-circular orbit.
Diagram C: probe P in a circular orbit with a dashed straight-line path directed at the centre of the planet.
Diagram D: probe P in a circular orbit with a dashed path that spirals inward to the surface of the planet.

content.text: For a circular orbit of radius $r$ the only speed that keeps the probe at that radius is $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$. Compare the probe's new speed with that value.
Decide whether the probe now has too much or too little speed to hold its orbit, then choose the sketch that shows what gravity does next.
D

The probe was in a circular orbit, so its speed matched the value needed for that orbital radius. Halving the speed makes the required speed for the same radius too large, so the probe no longer has enough speed to stay in orbit at that radius. Gravity pulls it inward; as it moves closer it speeds up, but the net result is a decaying spiral that ends with the probe striking the planet, as shown in diagram D.

items: 1 mark: selects the illustration in which the probe's orbit decays because its speed is now too low for that orbit, so it spirals in to the planet (correct response D).

content.text: Napoleon attacked Moscow in 1812 with his cannon firing a shot at an elevation angle of $40^\circ$. Napoleon then decided to fire a second shot at the same speed but at an elevation angle of $50^\circ$.
Which of the following observations would Napoleon expect to be true about the second shot when compared with the first?
Longer range
Shorter range
Longer time of flight
Shorter time of flight
Resolve the launch velocity: $u_y = u\sin\theta$ and $u_x = u\cos\theta$.
The time of flight follows from the vertical motion alone, $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, while the range follows from $R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$.
Check whether $\sin 80^{\circ}$ and $\sin 100^{\circ}$ are equal before you decide anything about the range.
C

$v_y = u\sin\theta$ increases as the launch angle increases from $40^\circ$ to $50^\circ$ at the same launch speed. The time of flight is $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$, so the second shot stays in the air longer. The greater height also compensates for the smaller horizontal component, so the range is unchanged for complementary angles, but the time of flight is longer.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the vertical component of the initial velocity is greater at $50^\circ$, so the time of flight is longer (correct response C).

content.text: Which of the following is LEAST likely to affect the amount of current produced?
The length of the rotating wire
The thickness of the rotating wire
The speed with which the wire is rotated
Whether the wire is oriented north-south or east-west

This experiment works because charge in the moving wire is pushed along the wire by $F = qvB$, so the emf depends on the length of wire that is moving, how fast it moves, and the component of the Earth's field perpendicular to that motion.
Ask which of the four quantities actually appears in that expression, and which does not.
B

This experiment relies on the Earth's magnetic field. Only the component of that field perpendicular to the plane of rotation changes the flux linking the circuit, so orientation north-south or east-west matters, as does the rate of rotation and the length of wire in the field. The thickness of the wire does not change the area, the rate of change of flux, or the resistance of this very low resistance circuit appreciably, so it is least likely to affect the current.

items: 1 mark: identifies that the thickness of the wire is least likely to affect the induced current, since the induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux (correct response B).

content.text: A single-turn coil of wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ at right angles to the plane of the coil as shown in the diagrams. The coil is then rotated in a clockwise direction as shown.
Which of the following shows the direction of current flow in the coil as it begins to rotate?

content.alt_text: Diagram A: a square coil in a downward field B, with the current arrow on the left side of the coil pointing into the plane of the page and the arrow on the right side pointing out of the page.
Diagram B: a square coil in a downward field B, with the current arrow on the left side pointing out of the plane of the page and the arrow on the right side pointing into the page.
Diagram C: a square coil in a downward field B, with both current arrows, left and right, pointing into the plane of the page.
Diagram D: a square coil in a downward field B, with both current arrows, left and right, pointing out of the plane of the page.

content.text: At the instant rotation begins the plane of the coil is perpendicular to $B$, so the flux through it is at a maximum and is about to start falling.
Apply Lenz's law: the induced current must flow in the direction that opposes that fall, so the field it produces must point the same way as the applied field $B$.
Use the right-hand grip rule to turn that field direction into a sense of circulation, then compare it with the arrows drawn on the coil.
A

At the instant rotation begins the coil is perpendicular to the field, so the flux through the coil is at a maximum. Rotating the coil reduces the flux, so by Lenz's law the induced current flows in a direction that maintains the flux, i.e. it produces a field in the same direction as the applied field. This requires the current direction shown in diagram A.

items: 1 mark: selects the coil in which the current direction, found by applying Lenz's law to the decreasing magnetic flux, matches the rotation shown (correct response A).

content.text: Which of the following graphs best shows the current flow in the galvanometer when the switch is closed?

content.alt_text: Graph A: current on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, showing a heavy straight line lying on the time axis, that is zero current at all times.
Graph B: current against time, rising rapidly from zero and then levelling off at a constant positive value.
Graph C: current against time, rising from zero to a maximum and then decaying back to zero.

content.text: Decide what happens to the current in the primary coil the instant the switch closes, and then what it does for the rest of the time the switch stays shut.
A secondary emf needs a changing flux in the core, $|\varepsilon| = N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. Evaluate $\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ while the primary current is steady.
A

Closing the switch makes a steady direct current flow in the primary coil. A constant current produces a constant magnetic flux, so the rate of change of flux in the core is zero and no emf, and therefore no current, is induced in the secondary. A transformer must be supplied with an alternating current, so the galvanometer registers no deflection, as in graph A.

items: 1 mark: selects the graph showing zero current, because a steady direct current in the primary produces no changing magnetic flux (correct response A).

content.text: Which of the following describes the order in which the rings P, Q and R reach the bottom of the magnets?
They arrive in the order P, Q, R.
They arrive in the order P, R, Q.
Rings P and R arrive simultaneously, followed by Q.
Rings Q and R arrive simultaneously, followed by P.
For each ring ask whether a closed conducting path exists around the ring, so that a changing flux can drive a circulating current.
Only the ring in which those currents can flow is retarded; use Lenz's law to explain the direction of the retarding force.
C

Ring P is plastic and ring R is a copper ring with a slit, so in neither ring can a significant current circulate; both fall freely and arrive together. Ring Q is a solid closed copper ring, so as it moves through the magnet's field the changing flux induces eddy currents in it. By Lenz's law these currents oppose the motion and brake the ring, so Q arrives last.

content.text: A transformer is to be designed so that it is efficient, with heating by eddy currents minimised. The designer has some iron and insulating material available to build the transformer core. The windings are to be made with insulated copper wire.
Which of the following designs minimises the energy losses in the core?

content.alt_text: Design A: a solid block of iron with insulated wire wound around it.
Design B: a stack of thin iron sheets separated by insulating material, with the insulated wire wound around the stack.
Design C: a stack of iron sheets separated by insulating material, with the insulated wire wound around the stack.
Design D: a bundle of iron rods separated by insulating material, with the insulated wire wound around the bundle.

content.text: The core loss is heating caused by eddy currents, which circulate in loops that encircle the magnetic flux in the core.
For each design ask whether such a loop can be completed: the laminations must be oriented so that the current is forced to cross from one sheet to the next.
Compare where the flux runs (along the axis of the winding) with the plane of the iron sheets in each sketch.
B

A changing flux in the core induces eddy currents that circulate within the iron and dissipate energy as heat. The size of these current loops is limited by laminating the core into thin sheets, with each sheet electrically insulated from its neighbours, and orienting the laminations so the loops cannot complete. This greatly reduces the effective area for circulating currents and so minimises eddy current heating, as in design B.

items: 1 mark: selects the design in which the core is built from thin iron sheets, laminations oriented so that currents cannot circulate around them, greatly reducing eddy current heating (correct response B).

content.text: Which of the following statements about cathode rays does this apparatus provide evidence for?
Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
Cathode rays are particles that have momentum.
Cathode rays can only be produced in vacuum tubes.
Cathode rays are waves of high frequency and short wavelength.
The paddle wheel is free to turn. Ask what has to be transferred from the cathode rays to the wheel for it to start spinning.
Momentum is a property of particles, not of waves, so use this to identify which statement this apparatus actually tests.
B

The paddle wheel is free to rotate and is set spinning by the cathode rays striking it. Transfer of momentum to the wheel requires the rays to be made of particles carrying momentum, so the apparatus is evidence that cathode rays are particles, not waves. The straight-line travel and the need for a low pressure are demonstrated by other pieces of apparatus, and the wave properties are contradicted by this observation.

content.text: Who was the first to correctly explain this relationship?
Planck, in 1900, when he suggested energy at the atomic level was quantised
Einstein, in 1905, when he suggested light was a stream of particles called photons
Rutherford, in 1911, when he suggested the nuclear model of the atom

Classical wave physics could not explain these curves, and predicted physically impossible results. Planck proposed that the energy of an oscillator is emitted or absorbed only in discrete amounts, $E = hf$, which reproduced the observed distribution and marked the beginning of quantum physics.

content.text: What element was most likely used to dope the silicon?
Boron
Germanium
Phosphorus
Sulfur
Use the position of the dopant level in the diagram: a level just above the valence band accepts electrons out of that band and leaves holes behind, so the semiconductor is p-type.

content.text: Which of the following correctly describes the movement of the electrons and holes in the rod when the magnetic field is applied?
They speed up.
They slow down.
They move to the same side of the rod.
They move to opposite sides of the rod.
The two carriers have opposite charges and, because together they make up the conventional current shown, they drift in opposite directions.
Apply $F = qvB\sin\theta$ to each carrier separately and compare the directions of the two forces.
C

Electrons are negative and holes are positive, and the two types of carrier drift in opposite directions because together they make up the conventional current. In $F = qvB\sin\theta$ both the sign of $q$ and the direction of $v$ are reversed for the two carriers, so the two forces are in the same direction and both carriers are swept to the same side of the rod. This produces the Hall voltage used in Hall effect sensors.

content.text: Use Kepler's Law of Periods to calculate Ganymede's orbital radius.

Use the law of periods as a ratio: write $\dfrac{r^{3}}{T^{2}} = \dfrac{GM}{4\pi^{2}}$ for Io and for Ganymede, then divide the two equations so that $G$ and Jupiter's mass cancel and only the ratio of radii and the ratio of periods remain.
Take care with the period ratio: Ganymede's period is four times Io's, not two, because the doubling in the stem happens twice. Then convert Io's orbital radius to metres before using it.
$r_{\mathrm{Ganymede}} = 1.06 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m}$, about $1.06 \times 10^{6}$ km.

Ganymede's period is twice Europa's and Europa's is twice Io's, so $T_G = 4T_I$ and the ratio of radii is $r_G = r_I \times 16^{1/3} = r_I \times 2.520$. Io's orbital radius of $421\,600\,\mathrm{km}$ must be converted to metres before use, so $r_I = 4.216 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$:
Jupiter's mass and $G$ cancel in the ratio, so neither is needed for this part; the value is independent of them.

content.text: State ONE such prediction.

The prediction has to be something that two observers, moving relative to one another, could in principle measure differently. State it as a comparison between what each observer measures, and make sure it concerns a time or a length rather than a vague statement about time 'passing'.
Time dilation: a clock moving at relativistic speed relative to an observer runs slow, $t = t_0/\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$.

Any one of three standard predictions earns the mark: time dilation, $t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}}$, in which a moving clock runs slow; length contraction, $L = L_0\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$, in which a moving object is shorter along the direction of its motion; or the relativistic addition of velocities, in which two velocities do not add classically. One mark is for a correct and unambiguous statement of one of them, and no calculation is required.

The model answer takes time dilation, and it is the natural choice here because a clock is the only one of the three effects that can be carried around the world and read on return, so it is the one that leads naturally into parts (b) and (c). The size of the effect also explains why verification had to wait: at a jet's cruising speed of $250\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ the fractional difference is only $\frac{1}{2}v^{2}/c^{2} \approx 3\times10^{-13}$, so over a single day a clock loses about $30\,\mathrm{ns}$, an effect no instrument available in 1905 could detect.

items: 1 mark: correctly states one prediction, for example time dilation, length contraction, or the relativistic addition of velocities.

content.text: Describe an experiment to test this prediction.

A test of time dilation needs a clock that has travelled and a clock that has not, both readable afterwards so that they can be compared. Ask what precision timing equipment could be carried on a commercial aircraft, and what should happen to the travelling clocks in the two directions around the world.
Do not stop at a description of the apparatus: the two marks need the stationary reference clock and the comparison after the journey, as well as the travelling clocks themselves.

Fly four caesium atomic clocks, all synchronised, around the world on commercial jet aircraft, two travelling eastwards and two westwards, and compare them on return with identical reference clocks that remained on the ground. The predicted time dilation for the aircraft's speed would be lost by the eastward-flying clocks and gained by the westward-flying clocks.

The experiment is the Hafele-Keating test of 1971, and the two marks are for identifying it and giving its features. Four caesium-133 atomic clocks were synchronised with each other and with identical reference clocks that remained on the ground, then flown right around the world on commercial jet aircraft, two eastwards and two westwards. On return the four travelling clocks were read against the reference clocks. The prediction from time dilation is that each flying clock runs slow, and that the effect is different in the two directions, because the eastward flights have a higher ground speed while the ground clocks beneath them are themselves being carried eastwards.

The observed result is what makes this a test rather than a demonstration: the eastward clocks arrived behind the reference clocks by tens of nanoseconds and the westward clocks ahead by a larger amount, in the directions and of the size predicted. A design earns full marks only if it includes a stationary reference, clocks that make the journey, and the comparison afterwards; a proposal to fly a clock and see whether it loses time, with no stationary reference, earns only the first mark. Note also that the prediction chosen in part (a) governs the design, so a test of length contraction would need a length standard, such as a fast particle's lifetime or a craft accelerating away from the observer, rather than a clock.

items: 2 marks: identifies the correct experiment and provides features and characteristics of it, for example the Hafele-Keating experiment with atomic clocks flown eastwards and westwards around the world on commercial jet aircraft compared with a reference clock on the ground.
1 mark: identifies the correct experiment.

content.text: Explain how technological advances since 1905 have made it possible to carry out this experiment.

Two things were missing in 1905 and both had to be supplied: a measuring instrument whose accumulated error was smaller than the effect, and a vehicle whose speed was large enough for the effect to be appreciable. Treat them separately.

For each, make the link quantitative where you can: how accurate did the clock have to be compared with the best clock of 1905, and how much of the effect would an aircraft travelling at a 1905 speed have produced?

Two advances are essential. First, caesium atomic clocks, accurate to about a nanosecond per day, made the accumulated difference in reading over a long flight large enough to be measured, whereas the mechanical clocks available in 1905 were far too inaccurate. Second, high-speed commercial jet aircraft flying at close to the speed of light relative to the ground gave the moving clocks the large velocity needed for the dilation to be significant, while the world-wide navigation network allowed their positions and hence their velocities to be determined accurately.

The first advance is the caesium atomic clock. The hyperfine transition of Cs-133 defines the second, and caesium clocks are stable to about $10^{-13}$, roughly a nanosecond a day, whereas the best mechanical clocks of 1905 resolved only about $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ in a day. That is a margin of about $10^{8}$, and it is what turned an accumulated difference of tens of nanoseconds into a measurable quantity instead of an unresolvable one. Precision timing equipment could also be carried in the aircraft and read on return, and the navigation network in use today means the flight velocities, and hence the difference to look for, can be predicted accurately.

The second advance is the high-speed commercial jet aircraft. The effect depends on $v^{2}/c^{2}$, so speed matters enormously: at $250\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ the fractional dilation is about $3\times10^{-13}$, giving roughly $30\,\mathrm{ns}$ lost per day of continuous flight, comfortably measurable with an atomic clock and, over the two or three days of a circumnavigation, tens of nanoseconds in total. The fastest aircraft available in 1905 could manage only about $50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which would have produced about $1\,\mathrm{ns}$ per day, nothing like enough. Three marks need two advances, each named and described and each tied to the experiment; the two above are the ones the mark scheme expects.

content.text: The idea of a universal aether was first proposed to explain the transmission of light through space. Michelson and Morley attempted to measure the speed of Earth through the aether.
Evaluate the impact of the result of the Michelson and Morley experiment on scientific thinking.

Start by stating the result precisely: what did the two groups measure, and what did they find when the apparatus was turned to lie along and then across the supposed direction of the Earth's motion through the aether?
A null result does not simply fail to detect something. Ask what the aether hypothesis predicted would be observed, and therefore which piece of evidence the experiment removed.

For the judgement, connect the discarded assumption of a privileged frame of reference to Einstein's postulates, and say why the community revised the way space and time were conceived rather than simply keeping the old model.
The null result undermined the aether hypothesis and led to a fundamental change in the way scientists thought about space and time, paving the way for Einstein's theory of special relativity.

Michelson and Morley found no difference in the measured speed of light for the apparatus aligned along and across the direction of the Earth's supposed motion through the aether. The null result removed the observational basis for the aether and showed that the speed of light is the same for all inertial observers, so there is no privileged frame of reference. Rather than the hypothesis being discarded, the way of thinking about absolute space and time changed fundamentally, so the result is a classic example of experimental evidence forcing a refinement of a scientific model.

content.text: In 1970 NASA launched Apollo 13, their third mission planned to land humans on the Moon. Half-way to the Moon a huge explosion crippled the spacecraft. The only way home for the astronauts was to fly around the back of the Moon and then fire the rocket engine to take the craft out of lunar orbit and put it into an Earth-bound trajectory.
At the completion of the rocket engine burn, mission leader Jim Lovell was heard to say, “We just put Isaac Newton in the driver's seat”.
Given that the spacecraft returned safely to Earth, justify Jim Lovell's statement.
Pin down the time frame first. The statement is about the period after the engine burn finishes, not the burn itself, so list the forces that act on the craft before and after that moment.
After the burn, apply Newton's first law: with no thrust, what must the craft keep doing? Then identify which force supplies the acceleration that bends that straight path into the transfer orbit.

The justification has to be an argument rather than a list. The crew chose the initial conditions, so explain how that transfers control of the trajectory to the laws of motion for the rest of the flight.
After the engine burn no further thrust was applied; the craft's path back to Earth was governed entirely by Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation, so Newton, not the crew, was 'driving'.

The powered manoeuvre was over once the engine burn finished. From that instant the only forces on the spacecraft were the gravitational forces of the Earth and of the Sun. Newton's first law says it must then continue in a straight line at constant velocity, while Newton's law of universal gravitation, $F = GMm/r^{2}$, continuously bends that straight path into a curved trajectory. The burn had been timed to place the craft on an Earth-bound transfer orbit, and from then on the Earth's gravity alone curved the craft's path back to Earth. In this sense the crew had set the initial conditions and Newton controlled the craft from then on, which is why Lovell said they had put Isaac Newton in the driver's seat.

content.text: Explain why only one tube jumped upward.
Trace the whole circuit, from one battery terminal through the link at the far end and back again. That tells you which way the current runs in each of the two tubes.
Once you have the two directions, use the rule for what parallel conductors carrying currents in the same direction do to each other, and then ask why only one of the two tubes can move.

The current travels down one tube and returns along the other, so the currents in the two adjacent parallel tubes are in opposite directions and the tubes repel. The forces are not symmetric: the repulsion between the whole length of the two tubes is far greater than the attraction to the short return leads, so the upper tube experiences a net upward force and jumps, while the lower tube is pushed down onto the rack.

Current leaves the $+$ terminal, runs the full length of one tube to the link joining the far ends, crosses the link, and returns along the other tube to the $-$ terminal. The two tubes therefore carry current in opposite directions, and parallel conductors carrying currents in opposite directions repel.

The repulsion acts along the whole 1 m of both tubes, so the upper tube is pushed up and the lower tube is pushed down, with equal and opposite forces as Newton's third law requires. Only one tube jumps because the lower tube is resting on the rack and is being pushed into it, while the upper tube is free to lift; the short link at the far end, whose current runs roughly across the tubes, is far too short to cancel the repulsion acting along the full metre. The mark scheme wants the repulsive force named AND the reason the conductor jumps upwards, so a response that says the current is switched on briefly and the tube jumps, or that attributes the jump to an induced back emf, loses the second mark.

content.text: What is the implication of this result for power distribution networks?
The current required in part (b) was enormous. Ask how the force between two neighbouring cables depends on the current they carry, and on how far apart they are.
Then turn that into something a network designer can actually do about it.

The very large currents in distribution cables produce large magnetic forces between them, so cables must be spaced far enough apart, or supported and arranged so that the forces between them are minimised.

The force per unit length between two parallel cables is $\frac{\mu_0 I^{2}}{2\pi r}$, so it grows as the square of the current and falls as the separation increases. Part (b) needed a current of order $10^{2}\,\mathrm{A}$ to produce a force of only $0.098\,\mathrm{N}$ on a 1 m length, so distribution cables carrying such currents exert forces of order newtons per metre on one another whenever they are only centimetres apart.

The implication is that cables cannot simply be bundled as closely as convenient. They must be kept far enough apart, or mechanically supported and arranged so that the forces between them are balanced and minimised, for example by transposing the conductors of a three-phase system so that each conductor spends an equal length of the run in each position in the cable. The mark scheme asks for any correct implication of this kind and lists 'cables must be far enough apart' and 'cables can be designed to minimise the effect of the force' for the single mark.

content.text: Identify the causes of the two main energy losses in the transmission of electricity between the power plant and the house.

There are two places where energy is lost between the plant and the house, and each has its own mechanism. Ask first what happens in the transmission lines, using $P = I^{2}R$ and remembering how large the current in them is.
Then ask what the alternating flux in the iron of a transformer core does to the core itself. The core is a conductor, and the flux through it is changing.
Resistive (Joule) heating in the transmission line wires, $P = I^{2}R$, and eddy current heating in the iron cores of the step-up and step-down transformers.

The first loss is in the transmission lines, which are ordinary resistors, so the energy lost in them is $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$. This is the loss that dominates, because the power is large and the current is set by the transmission voltage. Sending $1.0\,\mathrm{MW}$ at $3.3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V}$ needs a line current of only $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$, so a $10\,\Omega$ line loses about $92\,\mathrm{W}$; the same power delivered at $240\,\mathrm{V}$ would need $4.2\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{A}$ and lose about $1.7\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{W}$ in the same line. That is the whole reason the power is stepped up in the first place.

The second loss is in the transformers. The core is made of iron, which is a conductor, and the flux through it is changing as the primary current alternates. That change induces eddy currents in the core, which flow against the core's resistance and heat it, and hysteresis also removes energy from the core on each cycle. The core is laminated, and the laminations are insulated from one another, to break up the eddy-current paths; this reduces the loss but never removes it. Two marks need both mechanisms; a response naming only the wires, or only the transformer core, earns one.

content.text: Explain how the application of superconductivity could minimise energy loss in the system.
Begin with the definition: what happens to a material's resistance below its critical temperature? Then go back to the two losses you identified in part (b) and consider each in turn.

Do not stop at the definition. A mark is only earned when you say what happens to the resistive loss in the lines and to the eddy currents in the transformer cores, and remember that $I^{2}$ heating vanishes when $R$ is zero.

Below its critical temperature a superconductor has zero resistance. With $R = 0$ the resistive loss in the transmission line, $P = I^{2}R$, is eliminated, and the eddy current losses in the transformer cores are also greatly reduced, so much less of the generated energy is wasted between the power plant and the house.
The definition is that below a critical temperature a superconductor's resistance falls to zero, so the current it carries dissipates no energy at all: $P = I^{2}R = 0$ for any value of $I$.

Applied to the two losses from part (b): the resistive heating of the transmission lines is completely eliminated, because the cable now has $R = 0$ however large the current; and the eddy currents induced in a core made of a superconducting material meet almost no resistance, so their $I^{2}R$ heating also collapses. Together these remove almost all of the loss between the power plant and the house. The examiner report for this question records that a majority of candidates stated the zero resistance but stopped there, and that such responses did not earn the second mark, so the explanation of the effect on the losses is the point of the question. A complete answer may also note the trade-off, that the conductors must be held below the critical temperature, $77\,\mathrm{K}$ for niobium-titanium, so refrigeration cost and difficulty stand in place of the wasted energy.

items: 2 marks: links superconductivity to zero resistance in eliminating power loss.
1 mark: identifies what superconductivity means, that resistance falls to zero below a critical temperature.

content.text: Explain how an understanding of black body radiation changed the direction of scientific thinking in the early twentieth century.
Begin with what a black body is and what the measured intensity–wavelength curves looked like at a range of temperatures.
Then state the failure. What did classical wave physics predict for short wavelengths, and why is that prediction physically impossible?
Finally, name the specific proposal that did fit the data, and say which assumption about the nature of energy had to be abandoned for the change in the direction of scientific thinking to follow.
Black body radiation showed that classical wave physics could not explain the observed radiation curves, which led to Planck's quantised-energy hypothesis and the beginning of quantum physics.

A black body is a perfect absorber and emitter, and its measured intensity-wavelength curves at different temperatures could not be reproduced by classical wave physics, which predicted the physically impossible ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck's proposal that the energy of an oscillator is emitted or absorbed only in discrete amounts, $E = hf$, did reproduce the curves. The understanding of black body radiation therefore forced scientists to abandon the classical assumption that energy is continuous and to adopt quantised energy, redirecting physics away from classical mechanics towards quantum theory.

content.text: Using labelled diagrams and text, explain how superconductivity occurs according to the BCS theory.

Start with the simplest picture. Draw a regular lattice of positive ions and a conduction electron passing through it, label it, and ask what it does to the ions nearby — and what effective charge is left near the electron and in its wake.

That distortion of the lattice is quantised, and it is called a phonon. On a second labelled diagram show how a second free electron is attracted to the same distortion and becomes bound to the first.
The last diagram is the one that explains zero resistance. Show many overlapping pairs and the energy gap, then use that picture to argue why no conduction electron can be scattered and lose energy.

In the BCS theory a free electron distorts the positive ion lattice, creating a phonon which attracts a second electron; the two form a Cooper pair. Many overlapping Cooper pairs form a coherent condensate with an energy gap, so no low-energy excitation is available and the electrons cannot be scattered, so the resistance falls to zero below the critical temperature.

Below the critical temperature the ionic lattice of a metal is very slightly distorted by a passing conduction electron. The region of lattice near the electron is left with an effective positive charge and the region behind it with an effective negative charge. The quantised lattice vibration that describes this distortion is called a phonon. A second free electron is attracted to the same distortion, so the two electrons form a bound pair called a Cooper pair. Because the pair has twice the charge of an electron but relatively little extra mass it behaves as a boson. At low enough temperature very many Cooper pairs form and overlap, condensing into a single coherent state, and an energy gap opens around the Fermi level. Because no energy can be supplied to break the pairs, the electrons cannot be scattered by lattice vibrations, so their mean drift velocity is not reduced by collisions and the resistance of the material drops to zero.

content.text: On the grid provided, draw the straight line of best fit in the region where the photo-current varies greatest with photon energy.

The current is essentially flat near zero below about $1.2\,\mathrm{eV}$ and flat again on the saturation plateau above about $2.2\,\mathrm{eV}$. “Varies greatest” means the steep section in between, so fit only those points.
Carry the fitted line back to the horizontal axis, because part (b) reads the intercept from it.
A straight line of best fit through the points from about $1.70\,\mathrm{eV}$ to $1.90\,\mathrm{eV}$, extended back to meet the photon energy axis.

The points at and below $1.20\,\mathrm{eV}$ sit on a near-zero current and the points at $2.20$ and $2.50\,\mathrm{eV}$ sit on the saturation plateau, so neither set lies in the region of greatest variation. The usable points are $(1.70, 2.8)$, $(1.75, 4.0)$ and $(1.90, 8.0)$ in units of eV and microamperes.

Substituting the middle point, $4.0 = 26(1.75 - E_{0})$, gives $E_{0} = 1.59\,\mathrm{eV}$, and the line then predicts $8.0\,\mathrm{\mu A}$ at $1.90\,\mathrm{eV}$ as required, so the three points are collinear to within the resolution of the experiment. content.text: From the line drawn on your graph, estimate the minimum energy (work function) for photoelectric emission.
The minimum energy is the point at which the current falls to zero, so read off the photon energy at which the line from part (a) meets the horizontal axis.

Do not read the intercept off the lowest photon energy that happened to give a non-zero current. The small current at $1.20\,\mathrm{eV}$ is within the scatter of the experiment, and the extrapolated line is the better estimate of the threshold.
Remember what the quantity represents: this is the energy that has to be supplied to get an electron out of the metal at all, not the energy of a typical emitted electron.
About $1.6\,\mathrm{eV}$.
The threshold photon energy is the value of $E$ at which the line of best fit gives $I = 0$. Using the line from part (a), $I = 26\left(E - E_{0}\right)\,\mathrm{\mu A}$:

The same value is obtained by extrapolating the line to the axis by eye, which is what the question asks for, and the data support it independently: no current is detected at $0.50$ or $0.90\,\mathrm{eV}$, both below the threshold, and the current saturates near $9.4\,\mathrm{\mu A}$ well above it. This threshold is the work function $\phi$ of the metal, so $\phi \approx 1.6\,\mathrm{eV}$.

content.text: The experiment is repeated, but the intensities of the light sources are doubled. Predict the results of this new experiment by drawing a second line on the graph.
Intensity controls how many photons arrive each second; it does not change the energy of any individual photon, so the threshold energy found in part (b) cannot move.

With more photons arriving per second at every photon energy, more electrons are released per second at every photon energy. Work out separately what that does to the gradient of the line and what it does to where the line meets the axis.

A second straight line on the same graph that crosses the photon energy axis at the same point as the line in part (a), about $1.6\,\mathrm{eV}$, but with a steeper gradient than the first line. A line with a different intercept, or a horizontal line, is not acceptable.

Intensity is the energy delivered per unit area per second. For photons of energy $E = hf$ the number arriving per second per unit area is $I_{\text{light}}/(hf)$, so doubling the intensity doubles that number at every point on the horizontal axis.

The gradient therefore doubles, from about $26$ to about $52\,\mathrm{\mu A}$ per eV. The intercept is unchanged because below the threshold no photoelectrons are produced whatever the intensity, and the threshold is set by $hf_{\min} = \phi$, where $\phi$ is the work function of the metal. $\phi$ is a property of the metal and is unaffected by how much light falls on it, so the two lines must meet the axis at the same photon energy. A line that crossed the axis elsewhere would be claiming that the work function of the metal had changed, which the experiment did not do.
The new line would also reach the saturation current at a lower photon energy, but within the range of the graph the two features being tested are the unchanged intercept and the greater gradient.

content.text: Justify the line you have drawn in part (c).
Make the justification in two separate steps: first the effect on the number of electrons leaving the surface each second, then the effect, or lack of effect, on the minimum photon energy.

Be precise in the first step. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons incident each second, not the energy of each photon, and the current measures electrons per second rather than energy per second.

Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons striking the metal each second, so twice as many electrons are emitted each second and the photo-current at every photon energy is greater; the gradient of the line is therefore steeper. The minimum photon energy needed to release an electron depends only on the metal, not on the intensity, so the new line has the same intercept at $1.6\,\mathrm{eV}$.

Step 1, the gradient. The power delivered to the surface per unit area per second is the intensity. For photons of energy $E = hf$ the number arriving per second per unit area is $I_{\text{light}}/hf$, so doubling the intensity doubles that number at every photon energy. Each absorbed photon can release at most one photoelectron, and the $100\,\mathrm{V}$ on the grid collects essentially all the electrons that leave, so the photo-current $I = Ne$ also doubles at every photon energy. A graph of current against photon energy therefore has twice the gradient, which is exactly the steeper line required in part (c).

Step 2, the intercept. Below the threshold no photoelectrons are produced whatever the intensity, and the threshold is fixed by $hf_{\min} = \phi$, where $\phi$ is the work function of the metal. $\phi$ is a property of the metal and is unaffected by how much light falls on it, so the photon energy at which the current first becomes non-zero is unchanged and the two lines meet the axis at the same point.

A response that says only “more light means more electrons” earns the gradient point but not the intercept point. A response that argues the threshold falls because more energy is arriving confuses the total energy delivered with the energy of one photon, which is what an individual electron absorbs.

content.text: Calculate the rest mass of a proton found from this experiment.

Relate the relativistic mass from part (b) back to the rest mass with the Lorentz factor. Work out $v/c$ as a single small number before substituting, so you can see roughly how much smaller the rest mass has to be.

Evaluate that factor rather than dropping it. It comes out close to one but not equal to one, which is exactly why it is so easy to drop and report the part (b) value unchanged — but the two masses are genuinely different quantities and the mark is for using the relationship correctly.
$m_0 = m\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}} = (1.70 \times 10^{-27})\sqrt{1 - (0.20)^{2}} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, the rest mass, a little smaller than the relativistic mass found in part (b).

The mass from part (b) is a relativistic mass, so the rest mass follows from the Lorentz factor. Work out $v/c$ as a single number before substituting, so the size of the correction is visible: $v/c = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{7}}{3.00 \times 10^{8}} = 0.20$, so the factor is $\sqrt{1 - 0.20^{2}} = \sqrt{0.96} = 0.980$.
Because the factor is 0.980 and not 1, the rest mass is genuinely smaller than the relativistic mass; this is exactly the value quoted for the proton's rest mass, so the check is good.

content.text: During your study of geophysics you investigated the radiation reflected from various surfaces.

(i) is a first-hand practical, so name the two detectors you would really have used: one that responds to ionising radiation and one that measures the strength and direction of Earth’s magnetic field.

(ii) is about remote sensing. For each method be explicit about the three stages: what is sent towards the surface, what comes back, and which property of the returned signal is measured. The time of flight and the strength of the return are different measurements and give different information, so do not use them interchangeably.

items: (i) A Geiger-Muller counter connected to a scaler or rate meter to detect ionising radiation, together with a handheld magnetometer to measure the strength of Earth’s magnetic field.

(ii) Radiation reflected from Earth’s surface is used in remote sensing. Satellite radar instruments send microwaves towards the surface and detect the echo; the time of flight gives the height of the surface while the strength and character of the echo reveal whether the surface is water, vegetation, exposed rock or urban development. Ground-penetrating radar uses the same principle to map buried layers such as aquifers and mineral deposits, and naturally emitted or sunlight-illuminated radiation that is reflected is used to infer the density and composition of the underlying rock.

content.text: (i) The practical measures two quite different quantities, so it needs two different instruments. Ionising radiation is detected with a Geiger-Muller tube: an ionisation event in the gas produces a current pulse, which the scaler or rate meter counts, so the reading is in counts per second and is proportional to the radiation flux arriving at the tube. Earth’s field is measured with a magnetometer, which responds to the horizontal and vertical components of the field and reads out in tesla, so the field strength and its direction can be recorded at each site and compared with the radiation readings.

(ii) Remote sensing works entirely from the radiation that leaves the surface. With an active system such as satellite radar, the instrument transmits a pulse and times the echo. Since the speed of the wave in air is known, the round-trip time gives the height of the reflecting surface, and the fraction of the pulse that returns together with any frequency shift depends on how the surface scatters, which is what distinguishes water, vegetation, bare rock and built-up areas. With a passive system the surface is illuminated by the Sun or by its own thermal emission and the reflected or emitted radiation is measured; near-infrared reflectance separates vegetation types and thermal emission gives surface temperature, which is how fires and crop stress are mapped. Ground-penetrating radar is the same time-of-flight method at low enough frequency that the wave penetrates the ground and returns from buried interfaces, which is how aquifers, voids and ore bodies are found without drilling.

content.text: On 6 December 2004 a meteor exploded in the atmosphere above northern NSW. The blast was detected by sensitive microphones in Hobart at 5.25 am (AEST) and in Tennant Creek at 6.12 am (AEST).
AEST = Australian Eastern Standard Time

You do not need to know when the explosion happened. The explosion time is common to both paths, so subtract the two equations and the unknown disappears, leaving the extra distance equal to the extra travel time multiplied by the speed of sound.
Both times are quoted in AEST already, so the time difference is a pure difference in travel time. State the speed of sound you take from the Data Sheet before you substitute it.
(ii) is a design question, not a calculation. It needs three things: the structure of the instrument, what it measures, and how the measurements from several stations are combined into a position.

items: (i) About $2.4 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{km}$ from the explosion.

(ii) Seismic wave detection. A volcanic explosion generates seismic and infrasound waves that travel through the crust and the atmosphere. A network of monitoring stations records the arrival time of each wave; because the wave speed in rock is known and roughly uniform, the difference in arrival times gives the distance to the source, and the distances from several stations are plotted and intersected to fix the position of the explosion on a map.

content.text: Both detection times contain the same unknown time of the explosion, so subtracting the two travel-time equations removes it:

Using $331\,\mathrm{m/s}$ instead of $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$ gives $2.4 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{km}$ as well, so the answer is not sensitive to the choice of value for the speed of sound. A response that takes the ratio of the two arrival times, or that tries to guess the time of the explosion, cannot eliminate the unknown; that is the trap in part (i).

(ii) Any geophysical network is acceptable provided all three elements are given. A seismometer is a mass on a spring with a coil and a magnet, so relative motion between the mass and the case, produced as a seismic wave passes, induces a voltage that is recorded. Because the speed of seismic waves in rock is known and nearly uniform, the difference in arrival times at two stations fixes a hyperbola of possible source positions, and intersecting the hyperbolas from three or more stations fixes the epicentre. The same principle is used to monitor nuclear tests, and infrasound arrays apply it to explosions in the atmosphere.

content.text: The development of technologies that increased our understanding of Earth's magnetic field led to the acceptance of the principle of plate tectonics.
Evaluate this statement.

An evaluation needs all three of these in order: the technologies, the physical evidence they produced, and an explicit judgement about how far that evidence supports the statement. A description without the final judgement cannot score in the top band.

Be concrete about the technology. “Magnets” is not enough; the instruments that made the difference were fluxgate and proton-precession magnetometers carried on land, on survey ships and on satellites, which map the present field and its rate of change.
The strongest evidence comes from the sea floor. List the two things that can be measured in the ocean crust, the pattern across the ridge and the age, and say what each one rules in or rules out.
When you judge, ask what the measurements can and cannot do. They are direct and quantitative about where the continents are now; are they equally direct about the force that moved them?

The statement is largely justified. Magnetometers on land, in ships and in satellites now measure Earth's field precisely, and because the field has reversed many times, igneous rock laid down at each period records the field direction that existed when it cooled. The match between the age and orientation of the magnetic stripes in the oceanic crust and the age and fit of the continents gives direct, quantitative evidence that the continents have moved. The evidence is, however, indirect about the forces involved, so the statement is justified in its conclusion but is not a complete explanation.

Two conditions must be met for the field to be recorded: the rock must contain ferromagnetic minerals that align with the field as it cools, and it must not be subsequently reheated. Modern fluxgate and proton-precession magnetometers carried on survey ships and satellites map the present field and its secular change with great accuracy. When these measurements are compared with the remanent magnetisation of ocean-floor basalts, two striking results emerge. The stripes of alternating polarity on either side of each mid-ocean ridge are mirror images of each other, and the further a stripe is from the ridge the older it is; and the palaeomagnetic pole paths recorded in rocks on different continents line up when the continents are reassembled. Because a reversal changes the direction of the field rather than its strength, and because the magnetic stripes are quantitatively consistent with the rate of sea-floor spreading, the evidence is strong. The judgement, however, is that the technology provided the evidence but not the mechanism: it shows that the continents have moved but does not by itself identify the driving force, so the statement is justified as evidence but is not a complete explanation of plate tectonics.

content.text: The diagram below shows the deflection of a plumb-bob near a large mountain range. The diagram exaggerates the amount of deflection.

(i) The bob is not being pushed sideways by anything; it is being pulled. Ask what extra mass the mountain adds to the Earth directly beneath the plumb line, and in which direction that extra mass attracts the bob.

(ii) Compare what was predicted with what was observed. If the observed deflection is smaller than the mountains alone can explain, the assumption about the density of the material underneath must be wrong in a particular direction, and the direction of the error is the clue.

(iii) The pendulum is the key: the same pendulum, taken to different places, gives the same period only if the field strength is the same everywhere. Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ to connect the measured period to the shape of the Earth.

items: (i) The mass of the mountain range is additional to the normal Earth’s mass beneath the plumb-bob. The extra mass increases the gravitational attraction on the bob, so the resultant force on it is no longer exactly vertical but is tilted towards the mountain, and the plumb line is deflected in that direction.

(ii) The crust beneath the mountain must be less dense, or must extend to a greater depth, than was assumed. A low-density root displaces some of the dense mantle material, so the mass excess above it, and hence the deflection, is smaller than the mountains alone would predict. This is evidence that the continents float, that is, are isostatically supported on a denser mantle, as plate tectonic models predict.

(iii) Richer carried the same pendulum to a series of latitudes and measured its period at each. The period varied systematically, being longest near the equator and shortest at the poles, because $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ and $g$ is smallest at the equator where the Earth bulges. He had already been puzzled by the variation in the amplitude of his plumb line at each station. Since one unchanged pendulum gave different results in different places, the difference could not be the pendulum, so the field strength, and hence the shape of the Earth, varies with position and the Earth is an oblate spheroid rather than a sphere.

content.text: (i) A plumb line hangs along the resultant gravitational force on the bob. For a spherical Earth that resultant is the vector sum of the attraction of the whole Earth, which points at the centre, and the bob’s own weight, and the two are collinear, so the line is vertical. Under a mountain the mass distribution is no longer spherically symmetric: the mountain contributes an extra attraction directed horizontally towards the mountain. The horizontal component tilts the resultant, so the plumb line points towards the mountain. The angle is small, of order $\theta \approx a_{m}/g$ where $a_{m}$ is the horizontal acceleration produced by the mountain’s excess mass, which is why the diagram says it exaggerates the amount of deflection.

(ii) The prediction in (i) assumed that the only excess mass was the visible mountain. The measured deflection is smaller, so that model overestimates the horizontal gravitational field. The standard resolution is that the crust beneath the range is not as dense as the surrounding mantle: mountain building leaves a deep root of relatively light crust, and the buoyancy of that root displaces an equal mass of dense mantle, so the real mass excess is less than the visible rock alone. This is isostasy, and it is an important qualification to the simple argument that the mountains pull the plumb line. It also connects directly to plate tectonics, because it is the same buoyancy that carries the continents.

(iii) For a simple pendulum of fixed length $L$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. Richer found the period longest at the equator and shortest at the poles, and rearranging to $g = 4\pi^{2}L/T^{2}$ shows that $g$ is smallest at the equator. A sphere would give the same $g$ everywhere, so the variation proves the Earth is flattened at the poles, and the size of the variation is consistent with the small polar flattening of an oblate spheroid.

content.text: The images show a person's heart before and after a medical procedure.
(i) Think about what a scan of the heart has to show. A region that is not being supplied with blood will take up less of the injected material and will therefore look different from healthy tissue.

(ii) Choose from the table using two criteria: the radiation has to be able to get out of the body so that it can be detected outside, and the half-life has to be long enough to complete the scan but short enough that the patient is clear of radiation quickly.
A third, weaker criterion is that the isotope should be available in a form that can be injected and that reaches the heart, so read the table for more than just the numbers.

items: (i) A gamma-emitting radioisotope such as technetium-99m is injected into the bloodstream and carried by the blood to the heart. The gamma radiation emitted as it decays is detected by a gamma camera and used to build an image. The abnormal, poorly perfused region of the heart shows as a dark, or cold, area in the before image, which identifies the abnormality. After the procedure the same injection and imaging technique is repeated, and the after image shows that the previously dark region is now perfused, confirming that the blocked artery has been cleared and the abnormality corrected.

(ii) Technetium-99. It emits gamma radiation, which penetrates out of the body and can be detected externally to form the image, and its half-life of 6.02 hours is long enough to complete the imaging scan but short enough for the patient to be clear of radiation within a day and for the administered activity to decay away almost completely.

content.text: (i) The scan works because the tracer follows the blood. Once injected, the technetium-99m is carried in the bloodstream into the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle. Where an artery is blocked, the muscle beyond it receives little or no blood, so little tracer reaches it and the gamma camera records a region of low count rate, which appears as a dark or cold area on the image. That is the abnormality. Repeating the identical injection and imaging procedure after the procedure shows the same region now counting at the same rate as healthy tissue, which is direct evidence that the blockage has been cleared. Because both images are obtained in the same way, the comparison is valid, and the confirmation rests on the tracer rather than on the image itself.

(ii) Two properties decide the choice, and both are needed. First, the radiation must be detectable from outside the body, which rules out the alpha sources in the table, caesium-137 and uranium-238: alpha particles are stopped by a few centimetres of tissue, so they would irradiate the patient severely without ever producing an image. Second, the half-life must match the timescale of the scan. Carbon-11 at 20.30 minutes decays away before a cardiac scan can be completed, while iodine-131 at 8.04 days and thallium-201 at 3.05 days leave the patient irradiated for weeks. Technetium-99 at 6.02 hours fits comfortably: the scan takes tens of minutes, and almost all the activity is gone by the next day, which also minimises the dose to the patient.

content.text: The acoustic impedance of fat is $1.38 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
The acoustic impedance of bone is $7.80 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.

(i) Two media with different acoustic impedances do not pass all the incident energy across the boundary. The proportion reflected depends only on the two impedances, so identify them, apply the impedance reflection expression, and only then convert to a percentage.
The reflection is large here because the mismatch in impedance is large. If your reflected fraction comes out close to one half, check that the ratio has been squared once and not twice.

(ii) This part is about physics, not about instruments. For each technique identify what is sent into the body, how the image is formed from the differences in what comes back, and whether the radiation is ionising.

items: (i) About $48.9\%$ of the incident intensity, roughly $49\%$, is reflected.

(ii) X-ray imaging uses ionising electromagnetic radiation. X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons are decelerated in a metal target, and because they pass through soft tissue with only modest attenuation but are absorbed strongly by dense material such as bone and metal, the differences in absorption between tissues of different density and thickness form the image on film or on a detector behind the body. An endoscope uses no ionising radiation at all: a lamp or laser launches light down a thin optical fibre, which works by total internal reflection in its cladding to carry the light around corners, and the emerging light is imaged by the eye or a camera. X-rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves whose density-dependent attenuation produces a shadow image of deep structures, whereas endoscopes use visible light guided by total internal reflection to give a direct, real-time, colour view of internal surfaces, but only along the line of the tube and without irradiating the patient.

content.text: So about $48.9\%$ of the incident intensity is reflected and only $51.1\%$ is transmitted into the bone. The reflection comes from the mismatch in impedance: particle velocity and pressure must both be continuous across the boundary, and those two conditions can only be satisfied simultaneously if part of the wave is turned back. A larger mismatch reflects more, which is why the fat-bone interface is such a strong reflector and why it appears bright on the scan.

(ii) The comparison is made principle by principle. Both techniques send electromagnetic radiation into the body and detect what returns, but the physics differs at three points. Production: X-rays are produced by the deceleration of fast electrons in a metal target, which needs a large potential difference and a heavy target, whereas an endoscope uses an ordinary lamp or laser, whose output comes from a thermal or emission process. Transmission: X-rays are electromagnetic waves at frequencies of order $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, so they pass through soft tissue with only modest attenuation and are stopped by dense material, giving a shadow image of structures at depth; an optical fibre instead carries visible light by repeated total internal reflection at the glass-cladding interface, which works only for paths confined inside the fibre. Detection and risk: a film or detector records transmitted X-rays, and because X-rays ionise the tissue they carry a dose risk, whereas the light emerging from the fibre forms a direct, real-time, colour image of the surface along the line of the tube. The consequence is that X-rays image deep structure at the price of a radiation dose, while endoscopies image surfaces with no dose at all but cannot reach beyond the tube.

content.text: The images demonstrate advances in the use of ultrasound as a tool in medical diagnosis.
Describe advances in technology that have enabled the improvements shown in these images, and discuss current issues that have arisen from these advances.
Keep the two halves of the answer separate and label them. First the technology that produced the improvement, then the issue, and for each issue say what specifically causes it.

For the technology, name the change at the level of the hardware or of the signal processing: the number and arrangement of elements in the transducer, the frequency used, or what is done to the returning echoes. “Better computers” is too vague to score.

The strongest issues arise from the fact that ultrasound is not ionising and so has no dose limit. Follow that through and ask what happens to the way the technology is used when the usual restraint on scanning is removed.

The improvements came from piezoelectric crystal arrays replacing single-element probes, giving sector and phased-array images; from harmonic imaging and contrast agents, which resolve small lesions; from higher-frequency probes and improved electronic beamforming; and from colour Doppler and real-time 3D reconstruction. The issues are the cost of the equipment and the training needed, the dependence on a skilled sonographer, the fact that the images are operator dependent and less reproducible than other scans, the use of contrast agents which are not without risk, and the absence of any ionising dose limit, which can lead to indiscriminate scanning.
This part needs two clearly separated sections: the technologies that produced the improvements shown in the images, and the issues those advances have raised.

items: Technologies: piezoelectric crystal arrays replacing single-element probes, which steer the beam electronically and so give sector and real-time images; harmonic imaging, in which the receiver listens to the second harmonics generated in tissue, which sharpens boundaries and suppresses clutter; higher operating frequencies for structures close to the surface; improved electronic beamforming; and colour Doppler and three-dimensional reconstruction computed from the same echo data.

Issues arising from them: the cost of the equipment and of the training required, so the technique becomes concentrated in larger practices and patients in rural or low-income areas are scanned less often; dependence on a skilled operator, so images are less reproducible between operators than a CT or MRI scan and are harder to audit; contrast agents, which can cause reactions and are not risk free; and the absence of any ionising dose limit, which removes the usual brake on scanning and can lead to indiscriminate or unnecessary examinations.

Because ultrasound is non-ionising there is no equivalent of the ALARA principle that limits exposure, so the pressure to justify a scan falls on the judgement of the operator rather than on a dose constraint. That is the central issue the question is aiming at, and the advances listed above make it more pressing rather than less, because the images are now good enough to tempt repeated scanning and to broaden the range of examinations regarded as normal.

content.text: The following diagram shows the constituent parts of an MRI system.

(i) There are two components with quite different jobs. One creates and maintains a field; the other sends a signal at a very specific frequency and then listens. Say what each does to the hydrogen nuclei in the body.

(ii) A contrast agent improves a scan by changing the rate at which tissue recovers, not by adding contrast artificially. Work out which of the two tissues in the T1 curves is affected more, and what that does to the difference between them.

(iii) The comparison is with a technique that images the same organ by a different physical property. Ask what MRI measures in the body and what a CT scan measures, and then draw out the consequences for image quality, for patient risk and for the ability to image in any plane.

items: (i) The superconducting magnet assembly produces a very strong, uniform static magnetic field, which aligns the hydrogen nuclei, that is the protons, in the body along the field direction and sets the Larmor frequency at which they precess. The radio frequency coils transmit radio frequency pulses at that frequency, which resonate with the aligned protons and tip them out of alignment, and then detect the much weaker radio waves re-emitted as the protons relax back into alignment; those signals are used to build the image.

(ii) Gadolinium is introduced because it is paramagnetic and shortens the T1 relaxation time of the tissue it reaches, which increases the contrast between tissues in the image. The T1 curve of tissue A is shortened much more than that of tissue B, so tissue A becomes clearly distinguishable from tissue B and the abnormality is easier to see.

(iii) MRI distinguishes between soft tissues far better than a CT scan, because it detects the hydrogen nuclei in the body rather than the density of the tissue, so grey matter, white matter and different types of lesion, such as the small bright one indicated, can be differentiated directly. MRI is also safer, using only a magnetic field and radio waves rather than ionising X-rays, so it carries no radiation risk. It can image the brain in any plane without repositioning the patient, and it can show function as well as structure through techniques such as functional MRI and MR spectroscopy, whereas a CT scan shows structure alone.

content.text: (i) The magnet is a superconducting solenoid cooled to a temperature at which its resistance vanishes, so a very large current can be maintained in a compact coil and the field it produces is strong, uniform and stable. Its single job is to align the proton magnetic moments of the body’s hydrogen nuclei with the field and to set the frequency at which those nuclei precess, the Larmor frequency, which is proportional to the field strength. The RF coils then act as both transmitter and receiver at that frequency. In transmission they send a pulse whose magnetic field is perpendicular to the main field, which tips the aligned protons out of alignment; in reception, after the pulse is switched off, they detect the very weak radio waves emitted as the protons relax back, and the frequency, phase and amplitude of those waves encode the position and the type of tissue of the emitting nuclei.

(ii) Without a contrast agent, tissues differ in T1 only because of their local molecular environment. Gadolinium is strongly paramagnetic, so its unpaired electrons shorten the T1 of the water in its neighbourhood. The effect is not uniform: tissue A, in which the agent accumulates or through which it passes in higher concentration, has its T1 curve shifted much more than tissue B. The two curves are therefore pulled further apart, and a structure of type A lying next to type B becomes much easier to distinguish. That is why gadolinium is used where the abnormality is small and the surrounding anatomy would otherwise give poor contrast.

(iii) A CT scan measures the attenuation of X-rays, which is a function of density and thickness, so it shows bone clearly and shows soft tissue mainly as shades of grey that are hard to tell apart. MRI measures the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei, so it gives strong intrinsic contrast between grey matter, white matter, fat, fluid and many types of lesion, and the small bright abnormality beside the ventricle is directly visible. Two further advantages follow. MRI uses no ionising radiation, only a static magnetic field and radio waves, so there is no dose and no stochastic cancer risk, which matters for repeated imaging and for children. And the orientation of the image is not fixed by the physical orientation of a thin slice: because the position of each nucleus is encoded in the field gradients, the same data can be reconstructed in the axial, coronal or sagittal plane, or in any oblique plane, without moving the patient. Finally MRI can interrogate motion and function as well as structure, whereas a CT scan shows structure only.

content.text: Part A of the figure shows the absorption spectrum of light, produced by an incandescent filament, after it has been shone through a quantity of hydrogen gas.

content.alt_text: Three stacked absorption spectra labelled A, B and C with the wavelength regions violet, blue, green and red marked. Spectrum A, shone through hydrogen, shows four sharp dark lines. Spectrum B, Star Croesus, shows four sharp dark lines displaced to longer wavelengths than A. Spectrum C, Star Dromus, shows the same four features broadened into wide fuzzy bands. The diagram is marked DIAGRAMS NOT TO SCALE.

content.text: Also shown in the figure are the spectra obtained from two stars, Star Croesus in part B and Star Dromus in part C.
The dark lines are absorption bands in A, B and C.
Compare each star’s spectrum with spectrum A feature by feature: are the dark lines in the same places, are they in different places, or have they lost their sharpness?
A uniform displacement of every line and a loss of sharpness of the same lines are separate observations, so give a separate cause for each rather than one cause for both.

For (ii), ask what motion of the source produces each effect. A motion of the whole star along the line of sight shifts every line the same way; a rotation shifts the approaching limb one way and the receding limb the other way.

items: (i) Croesus: the absorption lines are displaced uniformly to longer wavelengths compared with A, that is, they are redshifted. Dromus: the lines are broadened into wide fuzzy bands rather than being sharp.

(ii) Croesus is moving away from Earth, since the redshift of its lines is the Doppler effect for a receding source. Dromus is rotating about its axis, since the broadening of its lines comes from equal and opposite Doppler shifts on the two limbs of the rotating star; Dromus is not in orbit around another star.

content.text: (i) The four dark features in spectrum A are the Balmer absorption lines of hydrogen, produced because the cool gas of the source absorbs at those discrete wavelengths. In spectrum B the same four features are still sharp and are all displaced in the same direction, towards the red end; that is a change of position with no change of width. In spectrum C the same four features sit in roughly the same places but each has been smeared into a wide band, so the positions are well defined but the widths are not.

(ii) A change of position with no change of width is a change of the whole pattern, which is what happens when the source as a whole moves along the line of sight: every line is Doppler shifted by the same fraction, so a line at wavelength $\lambda$ appears at $\lambda(1 + v/c)$ for a receding source. Hence Croesus is moving away from Earth. A change of width with little change of position is a different effect: a rotating star has one limb approaching and the other receding, so the line from the approaching limb is blueshifted and the line from the receding limb is redshifted, and the two overlap to give a wide band centred on the unshifted position. Hence Dromus is rotating rapidly about its axis, not orbiting. That the positions are unshifted as well as broadened is what rules out orbital motion, which would shift the whole pattern.
