content.text: Photographs taken of a one arcsecond by one arcsecond sector of the night sky show a group of fixed stars. Scales have been added to the photographs. One star appears to change position, swinging backward and forward over a period of one year. Two photographic negatives taken when the star was at the furthest ends of its apparent travel are shown.
The star is marked X.

The star swings backwards and forwards over a year, which is exactly one orbital period, and the two negatives were taken at the two extremes of that swing. The angle you measure on the plate is therefore twice the parallax angle, so halve it before using the parallax formula.
Part (ii) gives absolute magnitudes and a distance, so the distance modulus is the route in. Once you have the two apparent magnitudes, the ratio of the brightnesses follows from the magnitude scale.
Be careful with the logarithm: $5\log_{10}(d/10)$ is negative for a distance of less than 10 pc, so in this case the apparent magnitude is numerically larger than the absolute magnitude.

items: (i) About $4\,\mathrm{pc}$, that is about 13 light years.
(ii) About $1.7 \times 10^{4}$, that is roughly 17 000 : 1, in favour of Alpha Centauri A.

content.text: The factor of two matters: the two negatives are taken at opposite extremes of the apparent swing, so the measured separation is the full diameter of the stellar orbit projected on the sky, whereas the parallax angle is defined using the radius of that orbit, that is the distance from the Earth to the centre of the orbit. Measuring the total displacement and halving it is what converts one into the other. A student who uses $0.5^{\prime\prime}$ as the parallax angle gets 2 pc, and one who does not measure the displacement at all cannot start.

A ratio of brightnesses of about 17 000 to 1 is entirely consistent with the picture, because Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf of about 0.12 solar masses while Alpha Centauri A is a star similar to the Sun, and at the same distance the ratio of apparent brightnesses is the ratio of their luminosities. Note that the ratio does not depend on the distance at all: the distance modulus shifts both apparent magnitudes by the same $4.43$ and that term cancels in the difference, which is why the only quantities needed are the two absolute magnitudes.

content.text: The Hertsprung-Russell (or H-R) diagram relates the magnitude or brightness of stars to their spectral classes or temperatures.
Describe the technological advances that have made it possible to add astrophysical data to the H-R diagram, and explain how this data contributes to our understanding of stellar evolution.

This part has two halves that must be joined. First the technology, with enough detail to show what it measures that the older methods could not; then the effect the resulting data has on the picture of stellar evolution.

The technologies worth naming are the ones that changed the sensitivity or the range of wavelengths observed: photoelectric rather than photographic photometry, cooled detectors, spectrographs, and telescopes above the atmosphere.
The link to evolution is made by comparing populations, not individual stars. Once whole clusters and other galaxies can be measured, you can see the sequence of positions stars occupy as they age.

Photoelectric photometry, cooled CCD detectors, spectrographs on telescopes and space-based observatories such as Hubble have made accurate measurement of apparent magnitude, colour index, spectral class, radial velocity, binary orbit and asteroseismic oscillation possible across the whole Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Because the diagrams can now be populated for stars in other galaxies and for clusters of all ages, astronomers can compare the distributions and map the evolutionary paths off the main sequence through the giant, supergiant, white dwarf and neutron star regions, and so test models of stellar evolution.
A response that scores well separates the instruments from the inference.

items: Technologies: photographic plates have been replaced by photoelectric photometry and by cooled CCD detectors, which are linear and much more sensitive, so magnitudes and colour indices can be measured to a small fraction of a magnitude; spectrographs mounted on large telescopes resolve stellar spectra, so spectral classes, radial velocities and binary orbits can be measured; space-based observatories such as Hubble remove the atmosphere, so the same star can be measured at the same wavelengths from the ground and from orbit; and asteroseismology detects the surface oscillations of giant stars.

Contribution to understanding of stellar evolution: because the measurements are precise and repeatable, the H-R diagram can be populated not just for nearby stars but for clusters of every age and for stars in other galaxies. A cluster is coeval, so the position of every member in one diagram is a snapshot of a single age. Placing many such snapshots side by side produces the evolutionary track off the main sequence, through the giant, supergiant, white dwarf and neutron star regions, and the observed numbers of stars in those regions give the relative lifetimes. Binary and radial-velocity data then supply independent mass estimates, and asteroseismology gives internal structure, so the models that predict those tracks can be tested rather than merely assumed.

Without these technologies the diagram would have been a scatter of a few hundred poorly measured points confined to the Sun’s neighbourhood, and the evolutionary paths would have had to be inferred from theory rather than read from the data.

content.text: The graph shows the apparent magnitude of a supergiant star recorded over a period of time. The star is identified as a Type I Cepheid variable.

content.alt_text: Graph of apparent magnitude against time in days from 0 to 200, from -3.0 to -4.0, showing a repeating light curve with a sharp rise and a slower fall, with successive maxima about 70 to 75 days apart.

content.text: Read the period from the graph as the time between successive maxima, and remember that the light curve is of apparent magnitude, so moving up the axis means getting fainter, not brighter.
For (ii) the two dips in the second graph are not the same event. Ask which star is doing the blocking at each, and remember that the amount of light removed depends on which star is hidden.

For (iii), find the orbital period from the graph, convert it to seconds, and use the separation given. The orbital formula gives the sum of the two masses, so the mass ratio is what lets you get the smaller one.

items: (i) Cepheids obey the period-luminosity relation: the longer the period of the oscillations, the greater the star’s intrinsic luminosity, and so the lower its absolute magnitude. The period is read from the graph, converted to an absolute magnitude from the calibrated period-luminosity relation, and the distance modulus $m - M = 5\log_{10}(d/10)$ then gives the distance.

(ii) The system is an eclipsing binary. At A the brighter star of the pair passes in front of the dimmer one and is eclipsed, removing most of the light and producing the deep narrow dip. At B the dimmer star passes in front of the brighter one, so less light is blocked and the dip is shallower. At C, midway between the eclipses, neither star is in front of the other and both are visible, so the combined brightness is at its maximum and the curve is level.
(iii) About $1.2 \times 10^{32}\,\mathrm{kg}$, that is roughly 60 times the mass of the Sun.

content.text: (i) Cepheids are standard candles. Because they pulsate in a way that depends on their internal structure, the longer the period of the oscillation the greater the star’s luminosity and the lower its absolute magnitude, and the relation is close to linear in $\log L$ over about three orders of magnitude in period. The graph gives the period directly from the spacing of the maxima, about 70 to 75 days. That period selects an absolute magnitude from the calibrated relation, and the apparent magnitude is read from the axis of the same graph; the difference between the two is the distance modulus, from which the distance follows. A single star therefore yields both quantities from one light curve, which is what makes the method useful.

(ii) The two dips have different depths because the eclipses are different events. When the brighter star passes in front, it blocks the light of the dimmer star over a small disc and the combined light drops to a small fraction of its out-of-eclipse value, giving the deep dip at A. When the dimmer star passes in front, it blocks only its own small contribution, so the drop is much smaller, giving the shallow dip at B. Between and beyond the eclipses neither star is in front of the other, so all the light from both is collected and the brightness is at its maximum, which is the level section at C. The two dips falling at different times is itself the signature of an eclipsing binary, and the ratio of the dip depths is a measure of the ratio of the luminosities of the two stars.

The formula used is Kepler’s third law for two bodies, $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}r^{3}/G(m_{1} + m_{2})$, which gives the total mass and not the individual masses, so the ratio given in the question is essential. If one star has four times the mass of the other, the smaller one carries one fifth of the total, about $1.2 \times 10^{32}\,\mathrm{kg}$, which is of the order of 60 solar masses and so identifies the system as a supergiant binary of the kind plotted in the first graph.

content.text: During your study of From Quanta to Quarks you either performed a first-hand investigation, or you gathered information to observe nuclear radiation using a Wilson cloud chamber, or similar detection device.
Below is a true-size photograph in this type of device showing the tracks made by $\alpha$-particles.

In a cloud chamber the visible track is the record of ionisation along the path of the particle, so the appearance of a track tells you how much ionisation the particle makes and how much it is deflected.
For (i) you need two separate properties: one that explains why the tracks are thick and short, and one that explains why they run straight.
For (ii), predict the tracks of the other two radiations before you write anything. One of them is neutral, which is a surprise for students who expect every particle to leave a mark.

items: (i) The tracks are thick, dense and short, and are fairly straight. Alpha particles are relatively massive, so they move slowly and lose their energy quickly by ionising the air along their path, giving a dense trail of many ion pairs and hence a thick track. Because they are massive they are not deflected much by the atoms of the air, so the tracks are straight, and because they ionise strongly they have a very short range in air.

(ii) A beta particle. Beta particles are very light, so they are strongly deflected by the air molecules and their tracks are thin, faint and much longer, often showing a sudden change of direction when the particle suffers a close encounter with a nucleus. A gamma ray, having no charge and no mass, does not ionise directly and so leaves no track at all in a cloud chamber.

content.text: A cloud chamber makes ionisation visible: supersaturated alcohol vapour condenses preferentially on the ion pairs created along the path of a charged particle, so the droplets trace that path. The thickness of a track is therefore a direct measure of how densely the particle is ionising, and the straightness of a track is a measure of how much it is being deflected.

(i) Alpha particles are helium nuclei, about four times as massive as a proton and about 7000 times as massive as an electron. Their large mass means they lose energy very efficiently to ionisation, so a great many ion pairs are created in a short distance: thick tracks and a very short range, of the order of a few centimetres in air at atmospheric pressure. Their mass also means the impulses they receive in collisions with air molecules barely change their direction, so the tracks run essentially straight. A short, thick, straight track is the diagnostic signature of an alpha particle.

(ii) A beta particle is an electron or a positron, about 1800 times lighter than an alpha particle. The same collisions deflect it strongly, so its track wanders and often shows a sharp kink where it has come close to a nucleus and been scattered through a large angle. Because it is light it also penetrates much further before losing its energy, so the track is longer. It ionises much less per unit length, so the track is thinner and fainter. A gamma ray is an electromagnetic wave with no charge, so it does not ionise directly and leaves no track at all; it is detected only indirectly, through the secondary electrons it ejects, which do leave short tracks.

content.text: Naturally occurring uranium-238 spontaneously disintegrates according to the equation
The thorium radionuclide undergoes further decay according to the equation
Both equations are printed unbalanced, and that is deliberate: the missing mass numbers and atomic numbers are what the questions ask for. Write the two conservation equations for each decay.
In (i) only the alpha particle and the gamma photon carry mass number away, and a photon has zero mass number, so the mass number of the thorium follows directly.
In (ii) remember that a beta particle carries one unit of negative charge and no mass number, so the daughter has the same mass number as the parent and an atomic number one greater.
(iii) is about a conserved quantity, not a formula. Ask what is wrong with the beta spectrum that a proposed particle could put right, and then name the particle and the person who proposed it.

items: (i) Mass number 234, that is thorium-234.
(ii) Q is protactinium-234, $^{234}\mathrm{Pa}$.

(iii) Pauli pointed out that beta decay appeared to violate conservation of energy, because the emitted beta particles carried a continuous range of energies rather than one fixed energy, and he postulated the existence of an unseen neutral particle, the neutrino, carrying the missing energy and momentum so that both energy and momentum are conserved. Fermi then built a theory of beta decay in which a neutron converts into a proton by weak interaction, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, and showed that the resulting continuous beta spectrum and the observed energy distribution follow from the weak force.

content.text: (i) The first equation is $^{238}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{A}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + \gamma$. Conserving mass numbers,
so the nuclide is thorium-234. Conserving charge as a check, $90 = Z_{\mathrm{Th}} + 2$, so $Z_{\mathrm{Th}} = 88$, which is thorium, as expected.

(ii) The second equation is ${}^{234}\mathrm{Th} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z}Q + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e} + \bar{\nu} + \gamma$. Conserving mass numbers, $234 = A + 0 + 0 + 0$, so $A = 234$. Conserving charge,

and atomic number 91 is protactinium, so $Q$ is protactinium-234. The neutrino and the photon are electrically neutral and carry no mass number, so neither affects either balance. Students who forget the sign of the beta charge get $Z = 89$ and wrongly answer actinium.

(iii) In beta decay the emitted electron does not have one fixed energy; the beta spectrum is continuous from zero up to a maximum. If a neutral nucleus emitted only the electron, the energy of the electron plus the recoil of the nucleus would account for only part of the energy released, so the law of conservation of energy would appear to be violated, and the same argument applied to momentum. Pauli resolved this in 1930 by proposing a particle that is not observed: the neutrino, neutral and of negligible mass, which carries away the missing energy and momentum. It was not detected until 1956. Fermi then used the idea to build a quantitative theory of beta decay in which a neutron changes into a proton through the weak interaction, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, and the wide continuous range of electron energies follows naturally from the range of energies available to two light products. That is why the continuous spectrum became the strongest single piece of evidence for the neutrino and for the weak interaction.

content.text: An understanding of the nucleus led to the Manhattan Project, which was based in laboratories in Los Alamos between 1942 and 1945.
Describe the technologies developed from this project, and assess the significance to science and society of their applications.
Name at least two distinct technologies from the project and describe what each one actually does, rather than listing applications.

Split the significance into scientific and social, and support each judgement with a specific consequence rather than a general statement. “It was important for science” is not supported; “it made sustained controlled chain reactions possible, which is what both power generation and radioisotope production depend on” is.

An assessment has to acknowledge the double-edged nature: the same nuclear physics that produced the power and the medical treatment also produced the weapons. Say which side of that judgement carries the greater weight for you, and why.

Two technologies were the nuclear fission reactor and the atomic bomb, followed by nuclear power generation and radiotherapy. The reactor made sustained controlled chain reactions possible, giving nuclear power and radioisotope production for medicine and industry, while the bomb demonstrated the weapon potential. Scientifically these advanced nuclear physics and produced radioisotopes, radiation therapy and radiation detection and measurement, and produced power with a very high energy density and negligible greenhouse output. Socially they delivered reliable electricity and modern cancer treatment, but they also enabled nuclear weapons, and the legacy of weapons proliferation, accidents and radioactive waste makes the significance double edged and the subject of continuing ethical debate.
A high-scoring response develops two technologies in turn, then judges the significance of each against science and against society.

items: Technologies: the nuclear fission reactor, in which a controlled chain reaction of uranium-235 fissions releases energy as heat that is carried away by a coolant and used to make steam and generate electricity, and which also produces radioisotopes as a by-product; and the atomic bomb, in which the same chain reaction is allowed to run away in a fraction of a second, demonstrating that the energy released per unit mass of fuel is enormous and that the process cannot be contained once it has been initiated.

Scientific significance: the project established nuclear fission as a controllable process, which made sustained chain reactions, radioisotope production, radiation sources for medicine and industry, and radiation detection and measurement possible. It also produced power with an energy density orders of magnitude above any chemical fuel and with negligible greenhouse output, and it drove advances in reactor physics, materials and radiation therapy that continue today.

Social significance: nuclear power gives reliable baseload electricity with very low greenhouse emissions, and radiotherapy and diagnostic radioisotopes are now routine in medicine. Against that, the same work produced the first nuclear weapons, and the proliferation of weapons, the risk of accidents such as Chernobyl and the management of long-lived radioactive waste are continuing ethical and political problems. A justified assessment concludes that the significance is real but double edged, and that the social decision about how the technology is used cannot be settled by the physics alone.

content.text: For (i) the transition shown is an electron falling between two stationary states, so the energy of the emitted photon equals the difference between two energy levels. Use the Rydberg form of the hydrogen spectrum, with $n_{f}$ the final level and $n_{i}$ the initial one, and check that the bracket comes out positive.

For (ii) remember that the electron is a wave as well as a particle, so its wavelength follows from its momentum. Make sure the mass is in kilograms and the speed in metres per second before substituting.
For (iii) the question is why the orbit is stable, so the answer has to say what would happen to an orbit under classical physics and what the wave picture prevents.

items: (i) $\lambda = 4.86 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 486 nm.
(ii) $\lambda = 3.32 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 0.332 nm.

(iii) Bohr postulated that electrons occupy certain permitted orbits and do not radiate energy, but he could not explain why the electron does not spiral into the nucleus, since an accelerating charge should radiate. de Broglie’s hypothesis resolves this: the electron has a wave character, so the orbit is a standing wave in which an integral number of wavelengths fits exactly into the circumference. Such a standing wave carries no energy away, so the orbit is stationary and stable, and the condition that only integral numbers of wavelengths fit also explains why only particular radii are allowed, which was the empirical basis of Bohr’s atom.

content.text: The arrow on the diagram runs inwards from $n = 4$ to $n = 2$, so the final level goes in the first term of the bracket and the bracket must be positive for a real wavelength. The result lies in the blue-green part of the visible spectrum, which is the H-beta line of hydrogen and the fourth line of the Balmer series, consistent with a transition that ends on $n = 2$. Using $4$ and $2$ the other way round gives a negative bracket and no real wavelength, which is how students detect that they have read the arrow backwards.

Converting the electron mass from $9.109 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and using the given speed gives a momentum of $1.993 \times 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so the wavelength is about a third of a nanometre, comparable to atomic dimensions. de Broglie’s hypothesis, which part (ii) also asks for, is that if an electron has wave properties then only those orbits in which the circumference is an integral number of electron wavelengths are possible.

For (iii) the classical objection to Bohr is that an electron in orbit is accelerating, and an accelerating charge radiates; if energy were being lost the orbit would shrink and the electron would spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a second, which clearly does not happen. Treating the orbit as a standing wave removes the mechanism for the loss: a standing wave is a stationary oscillation pattern with nodes at its ends and carries no energy away, so the orbit neither decays nor radiates. The same wave picture also explains discretisation, because a standing wave of a given frequency has a definite size, so only particular orbit radii are allowed, and it is that empirical pattern of allowed radii that Bohr postulated without justification.

content.text: Logic circuits.
(i) Work through all four input combinations and evaluate the AND first, then apply NOT. Remember that NOT is the last operation, so it inverts whatever the AND produced.
(ii) The half-adder has two outputs, so two gates are needed. Decide which output is 1 only when both inputs are 1, and which output is 1 when exactly one input is 1.
An OR gate is the tempting substitute for the second of those, but it is wrong: it gives 1 when both inputs are 1, and that is not the sum bit for that case.
(i) $C$ is 1 only when $A = 0$ and $B = 0$; $C$ is 0 for all other input combinations.

(ii) A half-adder adds two single binary digits and produces a sum digit and a carry digit. It is built from an AND gate feeding the carry output and an exclusive-OR (XOR) gate feeding the sum output, with the two input bits connected to both gates.

items: Both input lines A and B branch to feed the two gates.
AND gate output: the carry digit, 1 only when A = 1 and B = 1.
Exclusive-OR gate output: the sum digit, 1 when exactly one of A and B is 1, and 0 otherwise.

content.text: (i) The expression is evaluated from the inside out. For each of the four input combinations, $A$ AND $B$ is 1 only when both are 1, and NOT then inverts it:

The output is therefore 1 for exactly one row of the table. A two-input gate whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 0 is a NAND gate, so $C$ is the output of a NAND gate with $A$ and $B$ as its inputs, and the circuit for (i) is a single NAND gate.

(ii) A half-adder adds two one-bit binary numbers. The four cases are 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 + 1 = 10, and in binary that last case is written as a 1 in the twos column and a 0 in the units column, so one addition produces two output bits. That is why it is called a half-adder: it adds single bits, not numbers, and a full adder is needed to add two multi-bit numbers. Looking at the same four cases, the output that is 1 only when both inputs are 1 is the carry, and that is the truth table of an AND gate, so the carry comes from an AND gate. The output that is 1 when exactly one input is 1 and 0 when both are 1 is the sum, and that is the truth table of an exclusive-OR gate. A correct circuit therefore shows the two input lines branching to feed both an AND gate and an XOR gate, with the AND output labelled carry and the XOR output labelled sum. Substituting an OR gate for the XOR is the common error, because it would give a sum of 1 when A = B = 1, where the sum bit must be 0.

content.alt_text: Operational amplifier symbol with inverting and non-inverting inputs Vi and output Vo, and a transfer characteristic graph of Vo (V) against Vi (microvolts). The graph is a straight line of gradient 1 passing through the origin from Vo = -15 V at Vi = -7.5 microvolts to Vo = +15 V at Vi = +7.5 microvolts, then flat, that is clipped, at plus or minus 15 V.

content.text: The transfer characteristic contains two pieces of information: the gradient of the central straight line, which is the open-loop gain, and the two flat sections, which show the output saturating.

For (i) the closed-loop gain of an inverting amplifier is set by a ratio of two resistors, not by the amplifier itself. Choose one resistor value, work out what the other must be, and remember the negative sign comes from feeding the output back to the inverting input.
For (ii) do not just say “amplified”. Sketch the shape, decide whether it is inverted, and check the peak value against the saturation levels shown on the transfer characteristic.

items: (i) An inverting amplifier: the input is connected to the inverting input through a resistor $R_{1}$ and the output is fed back to the inverting input through a feedback resistor $R_{2}$, with the non-inverting input earthed. A value of $R_{1} = 400\,\Omega$ and $R_{2} = 20\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ gives a closed-loop gain of $-R_{2}/R_{1} = -50$. The open-loop gain is the gain with no feedback path, read from the transfer characteristic as $15\,\mathrm{V}/7.5\,\mu\mathrm{V} \approx 2 \times 10^{6}$; it is very large but the output saturates for any input beyond a few microvolts. The closed-loop gain is much smaller but is set precisely by the ratio of the feedback resistors, and the feedback makes the amplifier linear, stable and free of saturation.

(ii) An inverted triangular wave of amplitude 15 V: the output follows the input multiplied by $-50$ but is flattened at $\pm 15\,\mathrm{V}$. With the triangular input shown, which rises to $0.6\,\mathrm{V}$, the ideal output would reach $-30\,\mathrm{V}$, so the output falls linearly to $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ by the time the input reaches $0.3\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t = 0.25\,\mathrm{ms}$, stays flat at $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ until $t = 0.75\,\mathrm{ms}$, and then returns linearly to $0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t = 1.0\,\mathrm{ms}$, repeating.

content.text: The transfer characteristic contains two pieces of information: the slope of the central straight line, which is the open-loop voltage gain, and the two horizontal sections, which show the output limited to about $\pm 15\,\mathrm{V}$.

So the amplifier is enormously sensitive without feedback, but it is useless as it stands, because the useful range of input is only about $\pm 7.5\,\mu\mathrm{V}$ and beyond that the output is clipped. Negative feedback is what makes it usable.

Any pair of resistors with $R_{2} = 50R_{1}$ is valid, so $R_{1} = 400\,\Omega$ with $R_{2} = 20\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ is one acceptable design; $R_{1} = 4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ with $R_{2} = 200\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ is another. The minus sign appears because the output is fed back to the inverting input, where it opposes the input, so an increase in $V_{i}$ produces a decrease in $V_{o}$. The closed-loop gain of 50 is fifty million times smaller than the open-loop gain of about $2 \times 10^{6}$, but it is determined almost entirely by the resistor ratio and is therefore accurate, repeatable and insensitive to the amplifier itself. The feedback also pulls the operating point back inside the linear range, which removes saturation.

For (ii), the ideal output is $V_{o} = -50\,V_{i}$, but $V_{o}$ cannot exceed $15\,\mathrm{V}$ in magnitude. The input peaks at $0.6\,\mathrm{V}$, for which the ideal output would be $-30\,\mathrm{V}$, so the output is clipped and travels along the $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ line for the middle part of each half cycle. The sketch must therefore be an inverted triangular wave with its peaks flattened at $-15\,\mathrm{V}$: on the rising part of the input the output falls linearly to $-15\,\mathrm{V}$, reaching the limit when $V_{i} = 0.3\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t = 0.25\,\mathrm{ms}$, stays at $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ until the input falls back to $0.3\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t = 0.75\,\mathrm{ms}$, and then returns to $0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t = 1.0\,\mathrm{ms}$.

content.text: Over the last ten years the ability to acquire, store and manipulate digital images has increased dramatically.
Describe the advances in semiconductor technology responsible for this increased ability, and explain how such changes have led to new consumer electronics applications.
For the technology, name the specific advances: the scale of the patterning, the clock speed, the memory density, and how components are combined on a single die.
For the applications, the marks are for the link, not the list. After each new product, say which advance made it possible.
Keep the order the question asks for: describe the advances first, then explain how they produced the applications.

Photolithography has moved from a few micrometres to tens of nanometres, so billions of transistors now fit on a chip; gigahertz clock speeds and larger memory densities have been achieved by scaling, CMOS and silicon-on-insulator designs, and system-on-a-chip integration places processor, memory and graphics on one die. The consequences are direct: a camera fits in a phone, a laptop now edits 4K video, a television is also a computer, and smart TVs, dashcams, digital voice recorders, medical imaging and augmented reality headsets have become ordinary consumer products that could not exist a decade earlier.
A response that scores well keeps the two halves in the order the question sets and links each application to a specific advance.

items: Advances in semiconductor technology: photolithography has moved from a few micrometres to tens of nanometres in feature size, so billions of transistors now fit on a single chip; clock speeds in the gigahertz range and much higher memory densities have come from continued scaling, from CMOS designs that keep both the static and the dynamic power low, and from silicon-on-insulator structures that reduce leakage and capacitance; system-on-a-chip integration places the processor, memory and graphics on one die, so data does not have to travel far.

How those changes produced new applications: because a complete computer now fits on one chip, a camera, a microphone and a GPS receiver fit inside a phone, and the phone is itself a consumer electronics product that could not exist a decade earlier. Because the memory and processing are cheap and fast, a laptop edits high-definition video rather than only storing it, and a television contains a computer, which is what makes smart televisions possible. Because the transistor count and the clock speed are high enough, real-time three-dimensional reconstruction from sensor data becomes affordable, which enables dashcams with lane detection, digital voice recorders, medical imaging systems and augmented-reality headsets. The link to state explicitly is that each of these products needs a combination of storage, processing and sensing that only became possible at these feature sizes, so the applications are a consequence of the technology rather than a parallel development.

content.text: Transducers and logic.
Part (i) is a classification task: decide which direction of conversion each device performs before you name any examples, and remember that the same device can be described in more than one way.

Part (ii) is a series circuit. The voltage across the resistor you want is the supply voltage minus the voltage already accounted for elsewhere, and the same current flows through every element in series.

Part (iii) needs two separate calculations, one for the switch closed and one for it open, and then the gate decides the output from the input voltage. Remember that the LDR and the fixed resistor form a potential divider, and check the input voltage against the logic threshold rather than against zero.

items: (i) An input transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, for example a microphone converting sound into a voltage, or an LDR converting light intensity into a change of resistance. An output transducer converts an electrical signal into a physical quantity, for example a loudspeaker converting a varying voltage into sound, or an LED converting a current into light.
(ii) $R = 220\,\Omega$.

(iii) Switch closed: LED current 20 mA, LDR 290 $\Omega$, so $V_{\text{in}} = 5 \times 290/(10\,000 + 290) = 0.14\,\mathrm{V}$, which is low, so G outputs 1. Switch open: LED current less than 0.1 mA, LDR greater than 1 M$\Omega$, so $V_{\text{in}} > 4.95\,\mathrm{V}$, which is high, so G outputs 0.

content.text: (i) The distinction is the direction of the energy conversion. An input transducer is at the front of a system: the quantity of interest is physical and the system needs it as an electrical signal, so the device converts physical to electrical. A microphone is the standard example, because a pressure wave that varies the capacitance of a capacitor, or that moves a coil in a magnetic field, becomes a varying voltage. An LDR is also an input transducer, but it converts light intensity into resistance rather than into a voltage, and a downstream circuit converts that into a signal. An output transducer is at the end: the system has an electrical signal and the quantity of interest is physical, so the device converts electrical to physical. A loudspeaker converts a varying current into a pressure wave, an LED converts a current into light, and a solenoid converts a current into a force. A device such as a loudspeaker microphone can be described as either, depending on the system it sits in.

(ii) The LED and the two resistors are in series with the $10\,\mathrm{V}$ supply, so the same current of $20\,\mathrm{mA}$ flows through $R$ and through the $200\,\Omega$ resistor, and the total potential difference across the pair is the supply voltage less the voltage at the node $V_{i}$:

The errors to avoid are subtracting $1.6\,\mathrm{V}$ twice, forgetting that the current is in amperes when using $V = IR$ so that $20\,\mathrm{mA}$ is $0.020\,\mathrm{A}$, and giving $420\,\Omega$ as the answer for the unknown resistor instead of subtracting the known $200\,\Omega$.

(iii) The LDR and the $10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor form a potential divider across the $5\,\mathrm{V}$ supply, so the input voltage of the gate is set by the ratio of the resistances, and the current through the LED in the isolator sets the LDR resistance from the table.

$G$ is drawn as a NOT gate, so a low input gives a high output and a high input gives a low output, which is why the two switch positions give opposite outputs. In both cases the input voltage is far from any threshold, near 0 V or near 5 V, so the result is not sensitive to the exact value of the LDR resistance. The circuit therefore isolates the switch electrically, so the 20 mA switching the LED cannot disturb the logic gate, while still passing the state of the switch to it as a clean voltage level.
